summary: Describes an experimental use of STUN that lets a client find out how the NATs and firewalls between it and a STUN server behave. This helps applications understand the kind of address translation and filtering they face. It was published as an experiment, not as a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This experimental STUN usage lets a client test how NATs and firewalls currently handle traffic. The results can change, so an application that needs reliable communication must have another method available.

subtitle: An experimental STUN usage for observing how NATs and firewalls behave during a test.

tldr.problem: Applications behind NATs or firewalls may not know why direct communication fails or how those devices currently handle traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A STUN client sends Binding Requests that test mapping, filtering, binding lifetime, hairpinning, and fragment handling.
tldr.outcome: The tests describe behavior at the time and ports tested, not a guarantee about future traffic. RFC 5780 is Experimental and is updated by RFC 8553.

facts.label: Client transaction rate
facts.value: No more than ten new transactions per second

today: RFC 5780 is an Experimental RFC and is updated by RFC 8553. Its text describes the discovery method as an experiment whose results do not guarantee future NAT behavior.

sections.title: What the Tests Can Tell an Application
sections.content:
RFC 5780 defines a STUN usage for discovering the observable behavior of NATs and firewalls between a client and a STUN server. It adds attributes to Binding Requests and Responses so the client can probe the path.

The results describe the devices' behavior for the server and client ports used at the time of the test. A NAT may behave differently later or under load. The RFC therefore presents discovery as diagnostic information or an optimization, not a replacement for a reliable fallback.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests show how a NAT or firewall behaves during a particular test. They cannot promise that the same behavior will continue later.

sections.title: The Behaviors the Client Can Test
sections.content:
Mapping tests check whether the NAT gives the client the same public address and port when it sends to different destinations. Filtering tests check which outside sources can send traffic back. These tests use STUN responses from a server's alternate address or port.

Other tests can estimate how long a UDP binding stays open, check whether a NAT sends traffic back to a client using its own mapped address, and observe how the NAT handles fragmented messages. A comparison of MAPPED-ADDRESS and XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS can also reveal a generic application-level gateway that changes address data.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can test whether its public address changes, which incoming sources are allowed, and whether an idle binding remains open. It can also test hairpinning and fragment handling.

sections.title: Mapping and Filtering Test Sequences
sections.content:
A mapping test starts with a Binding Request to the server's primary address. The response can provide an alternate address and port. The client then sends requests to the alternate address, first using the primary port and, if needed, using the alternate port too. Comparing the mapped addresses distinguishes the three mapping behaviors described by the RFC.

A filtering test asks the server to reply from an alternate address and/or port. If that reply reaches the client, it shows which sources the NAT currently allows. Filtering tests depend on earlier traffic, so the client should use a port without recent traffic; the RFC recommends leaving it unused for at least 15 minutes when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The client compares replies after changing the server address or port. Whether a reply arrives shows how the NAT currently maps or filters traffic.

sections.title: The Added STUN Attributes
sections.content:
CHANGE-REQUEST asks the server to change the IP address or port it uses for a response. OTHER-ADDRESS gives the server's alternate address and port, while RESPONSE-ORIGIN reports the source address and port actually used for the response.

RESPONSE-PORT asks the server to send a reply to a port on the client's address. PADDING adds data so a request can be large enough to test fragmentation. A request containing both RESPONSE-PORT and PADDING must be rejected with a 400 error.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attributes let a client ask for a response from another address or port, identify the response source, or add padding. The server can also be asked to send the response to a different client port.

sections.title: Client Limits and Security
sections.content:
Clients should not begin more than ten new STUN transactions per second. The RFC also advises pacing requests so retransmissions do not synchronize. Server support for some test attributes is optional, so clients must be prepared for an Unknown Attribute response in the cases specified.

The security discussion says altered responses can mislead a client about the STUN server. It also requires rejecting requests that combine RESPONSE-PORT and PADDING, which avoids an amplification attack aimed at the request source. A server may require authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients should pace their tests and handle servers that do not support an optional attribute. The RFC includes rules to prevent certain requests from making a server send amplified traffic.
